overviewHtml:
This ungraded knowledge check assesses your understanding of how to verify what an AI answer tells you. You'll be asked about confabulation and fabricated citations, lateral reading, the steps of a verification routine, and how stakes and specificity set the amount of checking.

Note: Use this to test yourself, review the feedback on any questions you miss, and retry until you feel confident before moving forward.

forms.stemHtml: An AI answer cites a journal article. You find the article, and its authors, title, and year all match. The article doesn't contain the finding the answer credits to it. Which kind of failure is this?

options.html: A fabricated citation, since the finding was invented
options.text: A fabricated citation, since the finding was invented
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. A fabricated citation points to a source that doesn't exist, and this article does exist. Crediting a real source with a claim it doesn't make is misattribution.

options.html: A misattribution, since the source doesn't say this
options.text: A misattribution, since the source doesn't say this
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! The source is real and correctly described, and it doesn't make the claim. That is misattribution.

options.html: A citation error, since a detail of the reference is wrong
options.text: A citation error, since a detail of the reference is wrong
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. A citation error is a mistake in the reference's details, such as the year or page number, and here those details are right. Crediting a real source with a claim it doesn't make is misattribution.

options.html: A spot check, since only one source was examined
options.text: A spot check, since only one source was examined
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. A spot check is a way of checking a sample of claims, not a kind of failure. Crediting a real source with a claim it doesn't make is misattribution.

forms.stemHtml: In a Stanford study, professional fact checkers judged unfamiliar websites faster and more accurately than historians and undergraduates. What did the fact checkers do differently?

options.html: They read each page more slowly and with closer attention
options.text: They read each page more slowly and with closer attention
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Reading the page closely is what the historians and students did. The fact checkers left the page and searched for what other sources said about it.

options.html: They examined each site's design and its "About" section first
options.text: They examined each site's design and its "About" section first
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. A site controls its own design and its account of itself. The fact checkers left the page and searched for what other sources said about it.

options.html: They relied on what they already knew about each topic
options.text: They relied on what they already knew about each topic
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The sites were unfamiliar, and prior knowledge wasn't the difference. The fact checkers left the page and searched for what other sources said about it.

options.html: They left the page and searched for what others said
options.text: They left the page and searched for what others said
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! This is lateral reading. The fact checkers scanned a page briefly, opened new tabs, and checked what independent sources reported about the organization behind it.

forms.stemHtml: An AI answer includes the sentence "A 2022 survey found that 40 percent of teachers use AI weekly." Which of these should you find in the original source to verify the number? (Select all that apply.)

options.html: The figure itself
options.text: The figure itself
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! The number may have been misremembered or invented.

options.html: The unit the figure is given in
options.text: The unit the figure is given in
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Units such as percent and percentage points are easy to swap.

options.html: The date the figure applies to
options.text: The date the figure applies to
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! A correct figure from another year may be presented as current.

options.html: What the figure counts
options.text: What the figure counts
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! "40 percent of teachers surveyed" is a different claim from "40 percent of all teachers."

options.html: Whether the assistant confirms the figure when asked
options.text: Whether the assistant confirms the figure when asked
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The assistant's confirmation comes from the same process that could have produced an error. The check is to find the figure, its unit, its date, and what it counts in the original source.

forms.stemHtml: You doubt a date in an AI answer, so you reply, "Are you sure?" The assistant apologizes and gives a different date. What have you learned?

options.html: That the first date was wrong and the second date is right
options.text: That the first date was wrong and the second date is right
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. In a 2023 study, assistants often withdrew correct answers when challenged. You've learned how the assistant responds to a challenge, and nothing about which date is right.

options.html: That the first date was right and the second date is wrong
options.text: That the first date was right and the second date is wrong
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The change alone can't show which date is right. You've learned how the assistant responds to a challenge, and nothing about which date is right.

options.html: How the assistant responds to a challenge, and little else
options.text: How the assistant responds to a challenge, and little else
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Assistants can withdraw correct answers under challenge and can also repeat wrong ones. Either date still has to be looked up outside the conversation.

options.html: That the assistant has now checked the date against a source
options.text: That the assistant has now checked the date against a source
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. A changed answer isn't a sign that anything was checked. You've learned how the assistant responds to a challenge, and nothing about which date is right.

forms.stemHtml: Which of these AI outputs most needs checking before you use it?

options.html: A statistic with a citation, for a report you'll publish
options.text: A statistic with a citation, for a report you'll publish
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! The stakes are high, and a statistic with a citation is a specific claim. Specific claims are where errors concentrate.

options.html: A list of possible titles for a team newsletter you edit
options.text: A list of possible titles for a team newsletter you edit
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. You can judge suggested titles by reading them, and little is lost if one is poor. A statistic with a citation in a report you'll publish combines high stakes with a specific claim.

options.html: A rewording of a paragraph you wrote, for your own notes
options.text: A rewording of a paragraph you wrote, for your own notes
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. You can judge a rewording of your own text by reading it, and the stakes are low. A statistic with a citation in a report you'll publish combines high stakes with a specific claim.

options.html: An answer in a very confident tone on any topic at all
options.text: An answer in a very confident tone on any topic at all
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Tone has no dependable link to accuracy, so it doesn't set how much to check. A statistic with a citation in a report you'll publish combines high stakes with a specific claim.

title: Verifying claims, sources, and citations
